# The Library Graph

> ✅ **APPROVED by the Human Operator, 2026-08-05.** Implementation may proceed (Constitution Art. II). Authored by the Engineer as Builder; audit and approval are separate roles (Art. 0, Art. III).
> 
> ⚠️ **One amendment (D9) was added after approval** and carries one open question. It does not affect any decision approved above it, and does not block Phase A.
**Human Operator, 2026-08-05:** *"The intention is to build this internally reinforcing graph, not a collection of utilities that act as spot fixes for problems we could have avoided through a correct architecture of the internal graph."*
This Epic establishes the data model the rest of ViLM derives from. It supersedes the parts of the naming and parsing specs that re-derived model decisions locally.
## The objective
|  | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| **O1** | Files named from the graph — studio as folder; performers, video name and studio in the name |
| **O2** | Complete video metadata held in the app |
| **O3** | A videos ↔ performers graph, with tags as connective tissue |
| **O4** | Performers fleshed out — metadata and photo galleries |
| **O5** | Action tags describe videos; attribute tags describe performers; never crossed |
| **O6** | A rich browse and consume experience driven by the graph |
| **O7** | Crowdsourced data is the primary source; manual entry fully supported |
| **O8** | Matched once, stays matched — never re-download the same record |
| **O9** | The renamer and parser are driven by validated studio and performer lexicons |
## The finding — graph-shaped intent in a non-graph representation
Measured against the schema at v23, 2026-08-05:
| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Tables in the catalogue | `assets`, `entity_profiles`, `smart_collections`, `scene_markers`, `playlists`, `playlist_items`, `deleted_entities` |
| Tables joining a video to a performer, studio, tag or series | **none** |
| How a video's cast is stored | prefixed **display-name strings** in a JSON array on the asset row |
| How "which videos feature this performer" is answered | every asset loaded into memory and string-matched, AKAs reconciled by hand (`ActorVideoCounts.build`) |
**The join key is a display name, not an identity.** That single fact explains a great deal of the existing surface area. Each of the following is a good implementation of a utility that exists to compensate for edges having no stable identity:
- the global entity-rename mechanism — renaming a node must rewrite every label that referenced it
- AKA reconciliation inside counting, filtering and matching — one person, several strings
- entity tombstones — a deletion cannot simply remove a node, because nothing points at it
- the studio-conflict audit — a video can carry two studios because nothing constrains cardinality
- the tag-case audit — `Scuba` and `SCUBA` are two nodes because the string *is* the identity
⚠️ **This is not a criticism of that code.** Each utility is well made and well tested, and the in-memory approach is fast at this scale. The point is narrower and structural: **they are all the same bug, and the model is where it lives.** Adding a seventh utility is cheaper this week and more expensive every week after.
### 💡 The reinforcing loop this Epic exists to close
The objective is not a set of features; it is a cycle in which each part makes the next stronger.
```javascript
1. Match a video to a source   ->  learn its studio, cast and release date
2. Confirmed nodes accumulate  ->  validated studio + performer lexicons
3. Lexicons resolve filenames  ->  un-matched videos gain identity fields
4. Better identity fields      ->  far better match queries
5. More matches                ->  back to 1, with a richer graph
```
Step 4 is measured, not assumed: a performer **pair** plus a studio collapses 233 candidates to 4, where 11 of 18 single-performer queries returned more than 100.
**Every verified defect below breaks a different step of this loop**, which is why they are one Epic rather than five tickets.
## ⚠️ Verified defects the current model produces
All four confirmed by reading code on 2026-08-05. The library volume was detached, so runtime confirmation against real data is still owed.
### V1 — Video enrichment results are discarded at save (breaks step 1)
`Asset.encode(to:)` writes 15 columns and omits four: `release_date`, `enrichment_state`, `enrichment_source`, `enrichment_checked_at`. `updateAsset` calls `asset.update(db)`, which builds its `UPDATE` from that container, so those columns are never written. Every acceptance path — per-video, batch, and the inspector — goes through it.
**Consequence:** the app cannot record that it already looked. This is precisely the "constantly redownloading the same data" the objective forbids, and it is also why release date — the field O1 and the age-at-release filter both need — never lands.
### V2 — A matched video cannot be remembered (breaks step 1 and step 5)
Schema v23 added `enrichment_source_id` to `entity_profiles` **only**. `Asset` has no such column. `PluginCandidate.id` is documented as *"the source's own identifier, opaque to core and passed back to fetch"* and exists at the moment of the match; the video acceptance path records `enrichmentSource` (the provider's name) and discards the id.
**Consequence:** every run re-searches by name and re-guesses which record was meant. The actor half of this was fixed in v23 — *"a validated match was being thrown away"* — and the video half was never done.
### V3 — Attribute tags are being written onto videos (breaks step 3 and O5)
Tags are flat `tag:`-prefixed strings with no kind. Nothing distinguishes a tag that describes an action in a video from one that describes an attribute of a performer, and nothing prevents the second landing on a video.
**Filename parsing actively creates this.** The parser assigns every tag segment it reads to the *video*, so an attribute term in a filename becomes a property of the wrong node. The graph is being actively mis-wired today, and the longer parsing runs at scale the more of it there is to undo.
### V4 — There is no studio lexicon (breaks step 2 and O9)
Studios are bare `studio:` strings. The provider resolves a studio name to a source id when querying, and discards it. There is no set of confirmed studios, so nothing can drive folders authoritatively.
## D1 — The nodes
`EntityProfile` is already documented as *"the profile record for an actor/studio/tag/series entity"* with ids prefixed `"actor:Name"`. **The node type therefore already exists and generalises**; studios and tags become first-class by using it, with no new table.
| Node | Today | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Video** | `assets` row | gains match identity (see D4) |
| **Performer** | `entity_profiles`, `actor:` | none — already complete and guarded |
| **Studio** | a bare string in a JSON array | becomes an `EntityProfile`, `studio:` |
| **Tag** | a bare string in a JSON array | becomes an `EntityProfile`, `tag:`, and gains a kind (D3) |
| **Series** | `Asset.videoName`, a free-text column | ✅ stays a column — see below |
✅ **DECIDED — Series stays a free-text column for now.** Only 5% of the library carries a series name and 4% a season/episode, the episodic grammar works from the string, and nothing else depends on it. Promoting it is migration cost paid before the content that needs it exists. **Revisit when film or episodic content actually arrives** — recorded here so the revisit is deliberate rather than forgotten.
## D2 — Edges are first-class, and identity is not a display name
An edge is a stored relationship between two node ids. It is **not** a label duplicated onto a row.
| Edge | Cardinality |
| --- | --- |
| Video **featured** Performer | many-to-many |
| Video **released by** Studio | many-to-**one** — a scene has one releasing studio |
| Video **described by** Tag | many-to-many, **action tags only** |
| Performer **has attribute** Tag | many-to-many, **attribute tags only** |
| Studio **parent of** Studio | hierarchy — a sub-label filter must find its parent's videos |
| Video **part of** Series | many-to-one, if D1's open question resolves to a node |
### ⚠️ Node ids must become opaque, or none of this holds
`EntityProfile.id` is literally `"actor:Name"` — **the display name is the primary key.** D2 cannot be satisfied while that is true: renaming a node would change its id, so every edge would still have to be rewritten, and D3's split of a colliding tag into two nodes is impossible because both would claim the same key.
**Therefore:** a node's id becomes opaque and stable; the display name becomes an ordinary attribute; and `prefix:Name` survives as a **lookup index**, not as identity.
|  | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity | `"actor:Name"` | opaque, stable, never re-derived |
| Display name | the key | an attribute, freely editable |
| `prefix:Name` | the key | a unique index used to resolve a name to a node |
This is what makes a tag split expressible at all: two nodes, the same display name, different kinds, different ids. It is also what makes renaming free rather than a cascade.
### What this buys, stated as the utilities it retires
- **Rename becomes free.** A display name is an attribute of a node, not the key. Renaming touches one row.
- **AKAs stop being a special case.** An alias is another name on the same node; the edge already points at the node.
- **Cardinality is enforceable.** A video cannot acquire a second releasing studio, so the studio-conflict audit has nothing to find.
- **Case collisions cannot occur.** `Scuba` and `SCUBA` cannot be two nodes when the node has an id.
- **Deletion is answerable.** What points at this node is a query, not a guess.
✅ **`deleted_entities`**** is not retired by this.** Cascading deletes answer *"what pointed at this node"*; the tombstone answers a different question — *"this was deliberately removed, do not re-create it on the next scan or import."* That intent has no other home, so the table **stays**, narrowed to recording intent rather than compensating for missing edges.
⚠️ **Migration is the hard half, and it is lossy in one direction.** Existing rows carry names, not ids. Promoting a name to a node requires deciding whether two spellings are one node — exactly the judgement the tag-case and studio-conflict audits already make, which means those audits become the migration's input rather than dead code.
## D3 — Tags have a kind, and the kind constrains the edge
**Human Operator:** *"Some tags describe the action in a video and some tags describe the attributes of the performer. We shouldn't tag a video with an attribute tag (a video isn't a redhead, an actor is)."*
A Tag node carries `kind`:
| Kind | Describes | Legal edge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **action** | what happens in a video | Video → Tag |
| **attribute** | a property of a person | Performer → Tag |
| **unclassified** | not yet decided | **no edge may be created** |
`unclassified` exists for migration only. It is deliberately unusable: a tag whose kind is unknown cannot be attached to anything, so the model never silently guesses.
### ⭐ AMENDMENT — kinds are extensible, and a kind declares what it may attach to
> ⚠️ **Added 2026-08-05 after approval, at the Human Operator's direction.** Needs confirmation into the baseline (Art. II).
**Human Operator:** *"Sounds like we do need another category or two. Maybe we make the model support expansion — new categories as needed."*
The measured vocabulary forced this: of 30 tags, `Compilation` describes the video's **form** and `Amateur` describes the **production** — neither an action nor a person. A two-kind taxonomy has nowhere to put them, and the category obviously grows (4K, POV, shot-on-film).
⚠️ **An open-ended list of kinds would destroy D3's enforcement**, which works only because each kind maps to a legal edge. So a kind is not a bare label — **it declares the node type it may attach to:**
```javascript
TagKind {
  name:      String    // "action", "video-attribute", "performer-attribute", …
  appliesTo: NodeType  // video | performer
}
```
New kinds are added as data, with no schema change and no new enforcement code: the write boundary asks the kind what it applies to and refuses anything else. **The rule "a video isn't a redhead" survives extension**, which is the property that mattered.
**Seed set:**
| Kind | Applies to | Examples from the measured vocabulary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | video | the bulk — 23 of 30 tags |
| `video-attribute` | video | form and production: `Compilation`, `Amateur` |
| `performer-attribute` | performer | 4 tags, 31 uses — hair colour, ethnicity, category |
💡 `attribute` is renamed **`performer-attribute`**, because with two attribute-ish kinds the bare word no longer says which node it describes.
### ⚠️ Consequence — the edge NARROWS the kind; it no longer DECIDES it
This Epic previously stated that *"the edge a source asserts already declares the kind"* — a tag on a performer is an attribute, on a video an action. **With two kinds targeting videos, that is no longer true.** A tag arriving on a video could be `action` or `video-attribute`.
**The amended rule:**
| After narrowing by the edge's node type | Result |
| --- | --- |
| exactly one kind matches an existing node of that name | resolve to it |
| the name is unknown, and several kinds could apply | **`unclassified`** — a pending association, straight to the worklist |
| the name is unknown, and only one kind targets that node type | resolve to it |
So performer-side tags still resolve automatically — one kind targets performers — while genuinely ambiguous video-side tags go to a human instead of being guessed. **That is the intended trade:** extension buys expressiveness and costs a little automatic resolution, and it costs it exactly where the ambiguity is real.
⚠️ **`unclassified`**** still forms no edge**, and a genuine name collision across kinds still splits into separate nodes.
### ⭐ AMENDMENT — identity is case-INSENSITIVE; display keeps the operator's casing
**Human Operator, 2026-08-05, on finding one tag stored under two casings (15 uses) and its differently-cased twin (1 use) in the live library:** *"Seems like a miss from the tag clean up renamer. Perhaps we need to evaluate those as the same thing — read as case insensitive, show with user preferred casing."*
⭐ **This is what finally delivers D2's promise.** D2 claimed *"case collisions cannot occur when the node has an id"* — but that was only true if something stopped two casings becoming two nodes in the first place. Case-folded identity is that something.
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Identity** | the case-folded name — two spellings differing only in case are **one node** |
| **Display** | `display_name`, in the operator's preferred casing |
| **Lookup index** | unique over (entity type, kind, **folded** name) |
The two spellings stop being a defect to detect and become a display preference. `TagCaseAudit` and `TagNormalizer` — which already compare case-insensitively and preserve internal capitals — become the **input to the migration's merge**, not an ongoing report.
⚠️ **Fold in Swift, not in SQL.** SQLite's `lower()` is ASCII-only, so a library holding names with accents or non-Latin scripts would still admit duplicates through an index built on it. The folded key is computed in Swift and stored, so the index is over a column whose correctness is testable rather than over a function whose behaviour depends on how SQLite was compiled.
**This applies to every node type, not only tags.** A performer or studio differing only in casing is the same entity, and the same rule resolves it — while `display_name` keeps the capitals that matter (`DeAnna`, `O'Brien`, `MacLeod`).
⚠️ **The migration must merge, not reject.** Promoting names to nodes will find existing case-variant pairs. They **merge**, carrying both sets of edges to the surviving node and keeping the more-used spelling as `display_name`. Rejecting them would strand real data on a technicality.
**Enforced at the write boundary, not in the UI.** A rule that lives in a view is not a rule — the parser, the enrichment merge and the CSV import all write tags too.
### Runtime ingest — a tag the lexicon does not know
⭐ **The edge a source asserts already declares the kind.** A tag the source attaches to a *performer* is an attribute by construction; one it attaches to a *video* is an action. The kind is not being inferred — it is being read off the assertion.
So `unclassified` is only for tags arriving with **no edge context**, which in practice means the filename parser: a bare token in a filename says nothing about what it describes. That is exactly the origin that should not be trusted, and it keeps the worklist small.
| Origin | Kind on arrival |
| --- | --- |
| Source, on a performer | `attribute` |
| Source, on a video | `action` |
| Operator, via a surface that names the edge | that edge's kind |
| **Filename parser** | **`unclassified`** — no edge context exists |
### A name that already exists as the other kind
Two nodes may share a display name (D3's split), so a bare string is ambiguous. **The edge resolves it — the same rule, applied to lookup rather than creation:**
| Writing | Resolves to |
| --- | --- |
| a tag onto a performer | the `attribute` node of that name |
| a tag onto a video | the `action` node of that name |
| no node of the required kind exists | **one is created, of that kind** — the edge already said what it is |
Tagging a performer with a name that currently exists only as an `action` tag is therefore **not** an error and **not** an auto-split of the existing node: it creates the `attribute` node beside it, leaving the existing node and its edges untouched.
⚠️ **T5 still rejects, and this does not weaken it.** T5 governs attaching a *specific node* of the wrong kind — an id, not a string. Name resolution happens first and can only produce a node of the correct kind; a caller holding an `action` node id and attaching it to a performer is still refused.
⚠️ **An unclassified tag still has to remember which video it came from.** T6 forbids the edge, so without somewhere to put the association the parser's finding is lost the moment it is made, and classifying the tag later would have nothing to attach.
**A pending association is recorded instead** — a `pending_tag_association` row, a (video, tag node) pair that is explicitly *not* an edge:
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Written when | a tag is discovered with no edge context |
| Counts as an edge | **no** — invisible to every graph query and to T6 |
| On classification | materialises into a real edge if the kind permits it; discarded with a report if it does not (an attribute tag parsed off a video) |
| Visible as | the classification worklist, with the videos each pending tag came from |
⭐ **This is the same mechanism the tag migration needs**, where legacy strings sit un-retired between phases 3 and 4. One staging concept serves both, and neither invents a second half-state.
For the unclassified case the rule is:
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Created** as an `unclassified` node | never dropped — discarding it loses what the source told us |
| **No edge** is created | it has no kind, so no edge is legal (T6) |
| **Surfaced** on the classification worklist | the operator gives it a kind, and the edge becomes possible |
| **Never auto-classified** | inferring kind from context is the guessing this Epic exists to stop |
| **Never a hard failure** | one unknown tag must not abort an enrichment run |
⭐ **And an unattended batch run writes no tags at all.** `VideoBatchPolicy.autoApplicableFields` already excludes them, recorded because *"a source tags far more finely than a person does — one real record carried seventy."* So unclassified nodes accumulate only from **reviewed** acceptances, which bounds the worklist to things a person already chose to bring in.
✅ **DECIDED — leave them; enrichment corrects them.** Attribute tags arrive authoritatively from the source, per performer. As each video is matched, its attribute tags are dropped from the video and the performer's attributes come from the source instead.
**Why not migrate them onto the performers:** an attribute read off a video is a guess whenever more than one performer is credited — a video tagged with a hair colour does not say which of three people it describes. Migrating would write a guess into the graph permanently, which is the failure this Epic exists to stop.
**Consequence:** the correction rides the enrichment campaign rather than being separate work, and the graph is wrong in a *known, bounded* way until that campaign completes. A video's attribute tags are therefore **not** authoritative and must never be promoted to a performer by any automated path.
✅ **DECIDED — kind lives on the node.** A genuine collision splits into two nodes rather than moving `kind` onto the edge. Kind-on-the-edge would mean the same node is an action here and an attribute there, which makes the constraint unenforceable at the write boundary — the property that makes D3 a rule rather than a convention.
## D4 — A match is an edge to an external identity, and must be as durable as any other edge
**Human Operator:** *"Once matched an actor and video should stay matched."*
Every externally-matchable node carries the same four fields, and **all four are persisted**:
| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `enrichmentSourceId` | the source's own id — the actual match |
| `enrichmentSource` | which provider concluded it |
| `enrichmentState` | matched / noMatch / ambiguous / needsReview |
| `enrichmentCheckedAt` | when it was last asked |
Performers satisfy this today. **Videos satisfy none of it** — see V1 and V2.
**The rule:** a stored `enrichmentSourceId` means later lookups *fetch by id*, never re-search by name. A re-search after a confirmed match is a defect, not a refresh.
**And the corollary that makes it worth doing:** when a match succeeds, fetch everything the graph will need *in that exchange* — cast, studio, date, tags, artwork, external links. A second call to fill a field the first call could have returned is the same waste in a different disguise.
✅ **DECIDED — a match is a settled state, skipped on every run, with visible provenance and an explicit undo.**
**Human Operator:** *"Skip entirely but include a 'matched to id _ or url _ on date ' type of label and let the user opt to undo the match to rematch or refresh. This can be the same mechanism as the current 'not found online, ignore in matching runs' mechanism."*
That mechanism is `EnrichmentState.unmatchable` — documented as *"a human decision to stop asking, and it is the only state a machine never assigns."* `matched` joins it as settled.
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| On a run | skipped, with a reason |
| In the UI | a provenance label — matched to *id* / *url*, on *date* |
| To change it | the operator explicitly undoes the match, returning the node to pending |
⭐ **This is already built and is inert only because of V1.** `VideoBatchPolicy.skipReason` already returns *"already matched"* for `.matched` and *"you ruled this one out"* for `.unmatchable`. It reads `asset.enrichmentState`, which is never persisted — so it is always `nil` and **every batch run re-processes every video.** Fixing V1 activates correct logic that already exists rather than adding new logic.
⚠️ **The provenance URL must come from the provider, not be built by core.** Core may not name a source (Plugin Architecture; the public-repository constraint), so it cannot construct a link from an id. The provider supplies the URL alongside the id, in the shape `EntityLink` already defines.
✅ **DECIDED — no backfill pass; existing matches re-populate as they are re-matched.**
Video matches to date are **unrecoverable** — there is no column they were stored in. Performers matched before v23 have a state but no source id; birth date covers identity for the 1,204 of 1,386 with full dates in the meantime.
A backfill would have to re-search by name to rediscover the id — which is exactly the re-guessing D4 exists to eliminate, and would produce matches of lower confidence than the ones being replaced. The honest path is to let the next match write the id properly.
⚠️ **This makes fixing V1 and V2 more urgent, not less.** Every enrichment run completed before that fix has to be run again.
## D5 — Validated nodes are the lexicons, and the parser resolves rather than guesses
**Human Operator:** *"This system prioritizes studios (which we have a lexicon of downloaded and verified studio names) as folder and actors (which we have a lexicon of validated and matched actor names in our library). These validated lists should be data sources in our renamer and parser."*
A node is **validated** when it carries a confirmed external identity, or the operator has confirmed it by hand. Validated studios and performers are the parser's and renamer's authoritative vocabularies.
**This reframes the parser.** It is not a regex reading strings; it is a step that **resolves filename tokens to existing graph nodes**. That is what makes the loop reinforcing — the graph teaches the parser, and the parser feeds the graph.
### ⚠️ This changes a recorded decision in the parsing spec
That spec resolved *"POSITION is the primary signal… vocabulary CONFIRMS or OVERRIDES, it does not decide"*, reasoned explicitly from *"a new or un-curated library has neither vocabulary"* — the hole that would otherwise make the parser work best on the libraries that least need it.
**That reasoning is still correct, and it is not what this changes.** The resolution:
| Situation | Primary signal |
| --- | --- |
| A validated lexicon exists and a token resolves to a node | **the lexicon decides** |
| No lexicon, or the token resolves to nothing | **position decides**, exactly as specified today |
The generality argument survives intact — a day-one library still parses by position — while this library uses what it has confirmed. **The parsing spec's D2 is amended, not overturned.**
✅ **DECIDED — verified means matched to an external studio id, and the folder tree has three dispositions.**
| Studio state | On disk |
| --- | --- |
| Matched to an external studio id | its own `Studio Name/` folder — the verified lexicon |
| Ruled out (`unmatchable`) — the source has no such studio | a shared unfiled folder — and `contentKind == personal` goes to a **separate** folder, never mixed with it |
| Not yet processed | stays in the library root, awaiting classification |
**Why this shape works:** a file's location states its processing status, so the migration is legible mid-flight — which matters directly for D6's resumability requirement. A partially-migrated library is readable rather than ambiguous.
✅ **DECIDED — two folders, not one.** A ruled-out studio is a lookup that came back empty; personal content is a privacy boundary that must never be sent anywhere. Sharing a folder would mix the two and make the boundary invisible on disk — and a boundary you cannot see is one that erodes. Keeping them separate also means a personal-content folder can be reasoned about, moved, or excluded as a unit.
## D6 — Order of work follows from the loop, not from feature appeal
The loop has a first broken link, and work upstream of it is wasted.
|  | Work | Why here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | Fix V1 and V2 — persist all Asset fields, add the video source id, guard against recurrence | Until a match survives being saved, every enrichment run destroys its own output. **No campaign should be run before this.** |
| **B** | Tag taxonomy (D3) and its enforcement | Parsing at scale before this multiplies mis-wired edges |
| **C** | Studio and performer lexicons (D5) | Nothing can drive folders or resolve tokens without them |
| **D** | Edges as first-class (D2), and the migration off name-keyed labels | The largest change; everything above narrows its scope first |
| **E** | Naming, parsing and relocation | Derived work — see the child specs |
| **F** | Graph-driven browse (O6) | Depends on B, C and D |
⚠️ **A is not a refactor and should not wait for the rest.** It is an active data-loss defect on the main path.
### 🚫 A rejected sequencing, recorded so it is not re-litigated
*"Do the rename first, it is the visible win."* Renaming reads identity fields out of the graph. Doing it before A means renaming from a record that could not keep what it learned, and doing it before C means renaming without the lexicons that decide folders. The files would be renamed twice, and the second pass is the dangerous one.
## D7 — Every value carries its source
**Human Operator:** *"Manual data entry is wonderful and must be supported but crowdsourced data from online sources is our primary source, even for manually added data."*
O7 is a **precedence** requirement, and precedence cannot be enforced without knowing where a value came from. Today it is enforced by field-by-field ordering — which works for studio and, as previously recorded, *"does not generalise."*
### Every value records one of three origins
| Origin | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `download` | a matched external source supplied it |
| `operator` | a person typed or accepted it |
| `filename` | read out of the file's name by the parser |
**Precedence: ****`download`**** > ****`operator`**** > ****`filename`****.** A parser result never overwrites a download or an operator edit. A download supersedes a filename read without asking, and supersedes an operator value only through the review surface — silently overwriting something a person typed is not what "primary source" means.
### ⚠️ It is ONE property, not one per field
Provenance covers every field, but it **must not** be modelled as a parallel `xSource` property beside each value.
`EntityProfile` is already at the Swift type-checker's practical limit: at 23 stored properties a full initialiser written as one expression *"exceeds what Swift will resolve"*, and adding a single field — `enrichmentSourceId` — broke three construction sites with an error that names neither the field nor reliably the right file. **Twenty-three parallel source properties would not compile, and the failure would not say why.**
Provenance is therefore a **map from field name to origin**, carried as one property and persisted as one column:
Each entry carries an origin **and the time it was set** — the timestamp is what lets a review explain *why* a value is being challenged, and costs nothing to store:
```javascript
provenance: [FieldName: (origin: FieldOrigin, at: Date)]
// studio      -> download   2026-08-05
// releaseDate -> download   2026-08-05
// cast        -> operator   2026-08-01
// title       -> filename   2026-07-22
```
⭐ **This is also the graph-consistent framing.** A value is an assertion, and an assertion has a source — the same shape as an edge having an identity. Provenance is not bolted onto the model; it is the model applied to attributes.
💡 **Follow-on, deliberately not now.** Clustering the enrichment triple and the career span into nested structs would relieve the type-checker pressure permanently. Recorded so it is not forgotten — **and explicitly not to be done during the migration work**, where it would churn every construction site at the worst moment.
## D8 — Relocation is a consequence of matching, not a campaign
**Human Operator, 2026-08-05:** *"As we match a video and confirm metadata, we should invoke the file renaming service to move that video to the appropriate folder with the appropriate filename."*
⭐ **This dissolves most of the migration risk rather than managing it.** Confirming a match is the moment a video's metadata is at its best and a person is present. Moving it then makes relocation an ordinary per-video step instead of a 2,101-file batch — the single most dangerous operation in the project.
| Property | Big-bang migration | Relocation on match |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resumability | must be engineered | free — each video is its own unit |
| Partial state | a failure mode to survive | the **normal** state, already modelled by D5's dispositions |
| Metadata quality at move time | whatever the batch found | the best it will ever be — just confirmed |
| Blast radius of a bug | the library | one file |
| Operator present | no | yes |
### The ordering that makes it safe
⚠️ **The match is committed first, independently, and is never undone by a failed move.**
1. Persist the match — source id, state, provenance, metadata. **Durable before anything touches the filesystem.**
2. If `contentKind` is declared, generate the target path from the graph.
3. Move the file, recording old and new **full paths** for reversal.
4. Update `relativePath`, re-key the fingerprint (as `FileRenamerService` already does).
A failure at 2, 3 or 4 leaves a correctly matched video sitting where it was. **A file that cannot move must never cost a match that succeeded** — that would reintroduce V1 by a different route.
### When a move does not happen
| Condition | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `contentKind` undeclared | stays in root; no grammar can be chosen without a kind |
| Studio not yet verified | stays in root, per D5 |
| Target name collides | skipped and reported — never auto-suffixed |
| Volume detached | queued; the match is already safe |
Each is a **queue**, not an error. The video is usable throughout.
### 💡 What remains of the bulk migration
A catch-up pass over videos matched *before* this existed — and, after decision 5's no-backfill, that set is small. **The bulk relocation stops being the primary path and becomes a backstop.** D6's dry-run, resumable and reversible requirements still apply to it, and they are cheaper to satisfy over a small set.
⚠️ **Reversibility is still required per move.** One file at a time is not self-evidently correct — 2,101 individually-wrong moves are still 2,101 wrong moves. The old→new full-path mapping is recorded for every relocation, batched or not.
## Schema changes
Additive only, matching the rule the backup feature depends on. Every column is nullable or defaulted so existing rows migrate without interpretation.
| Version | Table | Column | For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **v24** | `assets` | `enrichment_source_id` TEXT, nullable | V2 — the video match key |
| **v25** | `assets` | `provenance` TEXT, default `{}` | D7 |
| **v25** | `entity_profiles` | `provenance` TEXT, default `{}` | D7 |
| **v26** | `entity_profiles` | `tag_kind` TEXT, nullable | D3 — `nil` reads as `unclassified` |
**Also in v24, on ****`assets`****:**
- **`enrichment_url`**** TEXT, nullable** — the provider-supplied link behind D4's provenance label. Separate from the id because core may not construct a URL from an id: doing so would require core to know the source's address, which the public-repository constraint forbids. The provider supplies both or neither.
- **`content_kind`**** TEXT, nullable** — ⚠️ **this column does not exist today.** D5's folder disposition and T16's privacy boundary both depend on it. `nil` means *undeclared*, and per the naming spec kind is **declared, never inferred**, so nothing backfills it — 2,101 rows begin undeclared and the migration refuses to file any of them until they are declared. That is the intended behaviour, not an oversight: a guessed kind mis-files a video into the wrong grammar, and a guessed `personal` is a privacy failure.
**But undeclared cannot mean unreachable.** Two things make 2,101 undeclared rows tractable without inference:
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Fallback disposition** | An undeclared asset stays in the library root, un-relocated and fully usable. It is skipped by the migration and remains usable **locally** — playable, browsable, editable by hand. 🚨 **CORRECTION 2026-08-05:** an earlier version said "never blocked from … enrichment." **Withdrawn.** `nil` is the state all 2,101 rows begin in, so treating it as "not personal" would open the privacy boundary for the whole library on day one. **An undeclared asset reaches no external provider** — fail-closed, per Plugin Architecture D10.3a. Bulk declaration makes lifting that a single action, and relocation required declaration anyway. |
| **Bulk declaration** | The operator selects any number of assets and declares a kind for all of them in one action. |
⭐ **A bulk declaration is still a declaration.** The naming spec's *"declared, not inferred"* rules out the machine choosing; it does not require 2,101 individual choices. Selecting a thousand videos and declaring them `scene` is one operator decision applied a thousand times — which is what makes the rule affordable rather than theoretical. Measured shape supports this: only 5% of the library carries a series name and 4% a season/episode, so the overwhelming majority is one kind and the exceptions are few enough to pick out.
⚠️ **The UI may sort, group or filter to help the operator choose — it may never pre-select a kind.** A pre-filled default is inference wearing a declaration's clothes, and `personal` is the case where being wrong is unrecoverable.
⚠️ **Legacy rows carry no provenance, and must not be assumed.** An empty map means *unknown origin*, not `operator`. Anything else would invent a fact about 2,101 videos, and `unknown` must lose to `download` while never being silently overwritten by `filename`.
⚠️ **v24 must ship before any enrichment campaign**, or the campaign has nowhere to record what it matched.
### v27 — the edge tables (D2)
One table per edge kind rather than one polymorphic table: each carries a different cardinality constraint, and a shared table can enforce none of them.
```javascript
video_performer (video_id, performer_id)        PK(both)
video_studio    (video_id, studio_id)           PK(video_id)      -- one studio per video
video_tag       (video_id, tag_id)              PK(both)
performer_tag   (performer_id, tag_id)          PK(both)
studio_parent   (studio_id, parent_studio_id)   PK(studio_id)
                -- a ROOT studio has NO ROW here.
                -- Absence means root; there is no NULL-parent row.

pending_tag_association (video_id, tag_id)      PK(both)
                -- ON DELETE CASCADE on BOTH keys: deleting a video or a tag
                -- must purge its pending rows, or they resurrect as edges
                -- when the tag is later classified.
                -- NOT an edge. Staging for a tag discovered with no edge
                -- context, and for legacy strings between phases 3 and 4.
                -- Invisible to every graph query and to T6.
```
`video_studio`'s primary key on `video_id` alone is what makes T9 structural: a second releasing studio cannot be inserted. Foreign keys cascade on delete, which makes T12 structural rather than bookkeeping.
⭐ **`studio_parent`**** cascades too, and that is the correct behaviour.** `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `parent_studio_id` removes the **hierarchy row**, not the child's profile: the child ends up with no parent row, which *is* a root studio. So cascading promotes children rather than deleting them, with no application code, and `studio_parent` cascades like the rest. The mistaken reasoning was that deleting one studio silently deletes others — and with them every video–studio edge beneath, which is data loss dressed as referential integrity. Asserted in T12.
### v28 — opaque node ids
D2 requires `EntityProfile.id` to stop being `"actor:Name"`. This is the largest single migration in the Epic, and it has a consequence outside the database.
```javascript
-- additive first; the old id column is retired last.
ALTER TABLE entity_profiles ADD COLUMN uid TEXT;           -- opaque, every row
ALTER TABLE entity_profiles ADD COLUMN entity_type TEXT;   -- actor | studio | tag | series
ALTER TABLE entity_profiles ADD COLUMN display_name TEXT;  -- was encoded in the id

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX entity_lookup
    ON entity_profiles (entity_type, IFNULL(tag_kind,''), display_name);
```
⚠️ **The index is over (entity type, kind, name) — not over the name.** A unique index on name alone would reject D3's split, where two tags share a display name and differ only by kind. This is what reconciles D2's lookup index with D3.
⚠️ **v28 re-keys every edge table.** `video_performer`, `video_studio`, `video_tag`, `performer_tag`, `studio_parent`, `pending_tag_association` **and ****`deleted_entities`** all reference nodes and are re-pointed to `uid` in the same migration. Re-keying profiles without the edges orphans the entire graph — and leaving `deleted_entities` behind silently resurrects every deletion on the next federation sync, which is the exact failure that table exists to prevent (D9).
⚠️ **And it re-keys every photo on disk.** `ProfileImageNaming` derives each filename from `safeId(for:)` — the entity id with `:` replaced — so photos sit on disk as `actor_Name.jpg`. Re-keying nodes without renaming those files **orphans every profile photo and every gallery image in the library.** Renaming them, verified by count, is the step that makes v28 irreversible; it is gated on that count and asserted by T22.
⚠️ **The photo rename is two-phase, because disk and database fail independently.** Copy every image to its `uid`-derived name first, verify the count, and only then commit the id change and delete the old names. An I/O failure part-way leaves both names present and the database unchanged — recoverable by re-running. The reverse order would desynchronise disk from catalogue with no way back, which is the same class of failure as V1 at a larger scale.
💡 **This may deserve its own spec.** It is Phase D work with its own irreversible step and a blast radius reaching `ActorLibraryPackage`, `ActorPhotoScanner` and every image on disk. Recorded here because D2 depends on it; **sizing it separately is recommended** rather than letting it ride inside this Epic.
## Migration — names to nodes
The same four phases apply to performers, studios and tags, but they differ in difficulty and only tags can stall.
| Source | Becomes | Difficulty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `actor:` strings in `assets.tags` | Performer nodes + `video_performer` edges | **Low** — profiles already exist for most; AKA lists say which spellings are one person |
| `studio:` strings in `assets.tags` | Studio nodes + `video_studio` edges | **Medium** — the cardinality constraint bites: 1-to-1 today is unenforced, and the studio-conflict audit already lists every video carrying two. Those must be resolved **before** the edge table can accept them. |
| `tag:` strings in `assets.tags` | Tag nodes + `video_tag` edges | **High** — needs kinds first; see below |
⚠️ **The studio migration has a hard prerequisite the others do not.** `video_studio`'s primary key permits one studio per video. Every video the conflict audit flags will be **rejected by the schema**, so those conflicts are resolved first or the migration fails partway. That audit stops being a report and becomes a gate.
**Performers and studios cannot stall the way tags can** — they have no kind to classify, so their phases 1–4 run to completion once conflicts are resolved.
⚠️ **D3 and T6 create a contradiction that the migration must resolve, not inherit.** Existing video–tag associations are strings. Promoting them produces `unclassified` nodes, and T6 forbids an edge to an unclassified tag — so a naive one-pass migration would either drop every tag association or violate its own rule.
**Resolved: promotion and edge creation are separate phases, and the legacy strings survive between them.**
| Phase | What happens | The old strings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1 — Promote** | Every distinct name becomes a node. Tags enter `unclassified`. No edges created. | retained, still authoritative |
| **2 — Classify** | Each tag node is given a kind. The tag-case and studio-conflict audits are the input, since they already identify which spellings are one thing. | retained |
| **3 — Connect** | Edges created from the strings, now legal because kinds are known. | retained |
| **4 — Retire** | Strings dropped only once every association has an edge, verified by count. | removed |
### ⚠️ Legacy video tags that classify as attributes
A legacy video–tag string whose tag turns out to be an `attribute` **cannot become an edge** — T5 forbids it. A naive equivalence check in phase 4 would then never balance, and the migration would deadlock on exactly the data the model exists to correct.
**Resolved, and it is decision 2 arriving in the migration:**
| Phase | Behaviour for these strings |
| --- | --- |
| **3 — Connect** | No edge is created. The string is retained and counted as *pending enrichment correction*. |
| **4 — Retire** | The equivalence check **excludes** them: it balances action-classified associations only. |
| Afterwards | Each string is dropped when its video is matched and the source supplies the performer's attributes — exactly as decision 2 specifies. |
**The count is reported, not hidden.** "N video–tag associations are attribute tags awaiting correction" is a visible number that falls to zero as the enrichment campaign runs. A migration that silently discarded them would destroy the only record of work still outstanding.
⚠️ **Phase 4 is scoped PER TAG, never globally.** Gating the whole cleanup on *"zero unclassified tags"* would let one stubborn tag freeze the legacy representation for the entire library indefinitely. A tag whose edges are all created has its strings retired independently of every other tag; the migration is complete when the unclassified set is empty, but it makes progress the whole way there.
### The read contract while both representations exist
Between phases 1 and 4 a video's tags live partly in strings and partly in edges. Reads must not see either half alone.
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| A tag query returns | the **union** of `video_tag` edges and un-retired legacy strings, de-duplicated by resolved node |
| A filter counts a video once | whichever representation it matched, never twice |
| Writes go to | edges **only** — the strings are read-only from phase 1 onward, so the two cannot diverge |
| Phase 4 removes a string | only after its edge exists, so the union is unchanged by the removal |
⭐ **The union is what makes the migration invisible to the rest of the app.** Browse, filter and count behave identically throughout, which is what allows the migration to be paused indefinitely between phases.
**Nothing is lost if the migration stops between phases** — the strings remain the source of truth until phase 4 proves the edges reproduce them exactly. A tag left `unclassified` blocks only its own edges, and appears on a worklist.
⚠️ **Phase 4 is a one-way door and needs its own gate.** It is the only step that destroys the old representation, and per tag it must not run while that tag is unclassified or while its edge count disagrees with its string count.
### Where each constraint is enforced
Stating this matters because the two layers fail differently: a database constraint cannot be bypassed but gives a poor error, and an application check gives a good error but only binds callers that go through it.
| Constraint | Layer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One studio per video (T9) | **Database** — primary key | Structural; no write path can bypass it |
| Edge cleanup on delete (T12) | **Database** — cascade | Same |
| Tag kind vs edge kind (T5, T6) | **Application**, at the single write boundary | Needs the tag's kind, and must name the offending tag |
| Studio cycle prevention (T13) | **Application** | Transitive reachability; not expressible as a SQLite constraint |
| Reclassification lock (T14) | **Application** | Must enumerate the blocking edges to be actionable |
| Provenance precedence (T17) | **Application**, in the merge | It is a policy, not an invariant |
⚠️ **"Single write boundary" is a requirement, not a description.** Today the parser, the enrichment merge, the CSV import and the editor each write tags independently. T5 is only enforceable once they share one.
## D9 — The library is not static
> ⚠️ **AMENDMENT, 2026-08-05, after approval.** Added at the Human Operator's direction; needs confirmation that it is accepted into the approved baseline (Art. II).
**Human Operator:** *"The inventory of videos is not static. Videos will be deleted but actors shouldn't be automatically removed (that is a manual decision). New video files will be added and will need to enter the review and enrichment processes."*
Everything above is written around a 2,101-file corpus. That corpus is a **backlog, not the system.**
### ⭐ The migration is the steady-state process applied to a backlog
Because D8 makes relocation a consequence of matching rather than a campaign, a newly-added file and a legacy file take **exactly the same path**:
```javascript
scanned -> kind declared -> parsed against the lexicons -> matched -> relocated
```
**There is no separate import pipeline, and there should not be one.** A second path would drift from the first, and the corpus would be the only thing either was tested against. The backlog is simply the queue on day one.
### Arrival
`LibraryScanner` already inserts with `INSERT OR IGNORE`, so re-scanning is cheap and non-destructive. A new asset arrives `unreviewed`, with no kind, no match, and no provenance — which is exactly the state every legacy row begins in, and it needs no special handling.
⚠️ **The scanner only accepts ****`mp4`****, ****`mov`****, ****`m4v`****.** Every convention in the naming spec is written with `.mkv`, and film and episodic content overwhelmingly ships as `.mkv`. A file the scanner does not recognise never enters the graph at all — it is not skipped visibly, it is simply absent. **This must be fixed before film or episodic content arrives.**
### Departure — three different events, routinely confused
| Event | What it means | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The operator deletes a video | deliberate | remove the asset and its edges; **no node on the other end is touched** |
| The file is not on disk | **unknown** — a detached volume, an external move, or a real deletion | **never auto-remove the record.** Mark it missing and report it |
| The source no longer lists it | irrelevant | the local record is authoritative (D1) |
⚠️ **A missing file is not a deleted file, and the difference is the whole point.** This library lives on a volume that detaches often — the working agreement is *"build without it, verify when it returns."* A process that removed records for files it could not see would destroy the catalogue every time the drive was unplugged. **Absence is never evidence of deletion.**
❓ **Open — nothing detects a vanished file today.** The scanner only adds. A file deleted outside the app leaves a row pointing at nothing, and no `missing` state exists. Adding one is small; deciding what the UI does with it is the real question. **Needs a decision, and it does not block Phase A.**
  **✅Decision - **We should add a function within our check for changes utility that looks for new files to also update the library with the absence of files.
### ⚠️ Performers are never removed automatically
**A performer with zero videos survives.** Removing one is a manual decision, and this is a rule, not a default.
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Deleting a video | removes `video_performer` **edges**. T12 cascades edges, never the node at the far end |
| A performer reaching zero videos | **no action.** Not flagged for cleanup, not garbage-collected |
| Removing a performer | an explicit operator action, recorded as an `EntityTombstone` |
**Why the rule earns its keep:** a performer node carries enrichment state, a source id, a photo gallery, AKAs and a birth date — 1,204 of 1,386 have full dates. That is expensive to reacquire and independently valuable. **Video count is not identity.** A performer whose only video was deleted is still a person the library knows about, and deleting them would silently discard a match D4 exists to preserve.
⭐ **The tombstone already models exactly this.** `EntityTombstone` records *"an entity was deliberately removed"*, and exists so that federation sync can tell *"never had it"* from *"deleted it"* — without which a union always resurrects the deletion. It is already the record of a manual decision, which is what D9 requires. This also confirms the earlier ruling that `deleted_entities` survives D2 rather than being retired by cascades.
⚠️ **Tombstones are keyed by ****`actor:Name`**** and must be re-keyed by v28.** A tombstone that still names an old-style id after nodes become opaque stops matching the entity it was meant to suppress, and the deletion resurrects on the next sync — the precise failure the table was built to prevent.
## Test strategy (Constitution Art. III)
- **T1 — Nothing is lost on save.** An `Asset` populated in every field round-trips through the store unchanged. Asserted field by field, not by spot check.
- **T2 — The guard holds.** A reflective field-count test over `Asset` fails when a property is added, and names every copy site — mirroring the existing `EntityProfile` guard, which has already prevented several silent losses.
- **T3 — A match survives.** After acceptance, the source id, state and timestamp are readable from a freshly-opened store.
- **T4 — A match is not re-searched, and failure is handled.** With a stored source id, a second pass fetches by id and issues no name search — asserted against a provider double that **fails the test if a search is attempted**. The same double must also exercise, as distinct cases: the id no longer existing at the source, a network failure, a rate-limit response, and a malformed payload. In every one, the stored match and the local record survive unchanged and the failure is reported — a lookup that cannot complete must never downgrade a settled match.
- **T5 — Attribute tags cannot reach a video.** Every write path — parser, enrichment merge, CSV import, manual edit — rejects an attribute tag on a video and an action tag on a performer.
- **T6 — Unclassified tags attach to nothing.** Creating a Video→Tag or Performer→Tag edge whose tag has `kind == unclassified` fails, and the failure names the tag. A migration that promotes a name to an unclassified node therefore leaves zero edges behind it, and the count of unclassified nodes is reported as a worklist rather than silently tolerated. 
- **T7 — Renaming a node moves no edges.** After a rename, every edge that pointed at the node still does, and nothing else changed.
- **T8 — An alias is not a second node.** A video credited under an alias resolves to the same performer node as the canonical name.
- **T9 — Cardinality is enforced.** A video cannot acquire a second releasing studio.
- **T10 — Migration is reversible and reports what it could not decide.** Promoting names to nodes never merges two nodes silently; ambiguous cases become a worklist.
- **T11 — A sub-label finds its parent's videos.** A filter on a parent studio includes videos released under its children.
- **T12 — Deleting a node leaves no orphan edges, and deletes nothing else.** Deleting a performer, studio or tag removes every edge that pointed at it; no video loses its own record; and what was removed is reported rather than discovered later. Asserted for each node type. **Deleting a parent studio promotes its children to root studios and deletes none of them**, nor any of their video edges.
- **T13 — A studio hierarchy cannot contain a cycle.** Setting a parent that would make a studio its own ancestor — directly or transitively — fails, and the failure names the path. Without this a parent-studio filter recurses forever.
- **T14 — A tag's kind cannot be changed out from under its edges.** Reclassifying an action tag as an attribute fails while Video→Tag edges exist, and the failure lists them; the operator moves or drops the edges first. This is the reclassification case, distinct from T5's write-boundary check.
- **T15 — Undoing a match returns the node to pending and keeps the operator's work.** After an undo, `enrichmentState` is pending, `enrichmentSourceId` is cleared, and every field whose provenance is `operator` is **unchanged**. Undo reverses the match, not the human's edits.
- **T16 — Personal content never reaches a provider.** With `contentKind == personal`, a batch run and a per-video lookup both refuse before any request is constructed. Asserted against a provider double that **fails the test if it is called at all** — structural exclusion, not a skipped iteration.
- **T17a — A download disagreeing with an operator value writes nothing.** The stored value survives, the node enters `needsReview`, and the download's value exists only as a proposal until accepted. Accepting rewrites the value and flips its provenance to `download`; rejecting leaves both the value and its provenance untouched.
- **T17 — Precedence is enforced by provenance, not by ordering.** A `filename` value never overwrites a `download` or `operator` value. A `download` supersedes `filename` silently and `operator` only through review. A field with unknown provenance loses to `download` and is never silently overwritten by `filename`. Asserted for every ordering of arrival, because ordering is precisely what must stop mattering.
- **T19 — A single-field update merges provenance rather than replacing it.** Writing one field updates that field's origin and leaves every other entry in the map untouched. Asserted by writing each field in turn and checking the whole map after each — a serialized map is exactly the shape that fails this way, silently, and only for the fields nobody looked at.
- **T20 — The migration is reversible until phase 4, and phase 4 is gated per tag.** Stopping after any of phases 1–3 leaves the legacy strings authoritative and the library fully usable. For a given tag, phase 4 refuses to run while that tag is `unclassified`, and verifies its edge count reproduces its string associations before dropping them. **Asserted explicitly: video strings whose tag is ****`attribute`****-classified are excluded from that equivalence check and are not dropped** — without which a single attribute tag deadlocks the tag it belongs to.
- **T25 — Bulk kind declaration is all-or-nothing and validated.** Declaring a kind across a selection either applies to every asset or to none; a rejected member (already declared, or missing) fails the batch with a reason rather than leaving it half applied. No path assigns a kind the operator did not choose — including the empty selection.
- **T26 — Opaque ids migrate without losing anything.** After v28 every profile retains every field, the (kind, name) lookup index resolves each former `prefix:Name` to the right node, two same-named tags of different kinds both resolve, and the row count is unchanged. Run against a fixture containing a deliberate name collision.
- **T34 — The scanner accepts every container the conventions use.** A `.mkv` file is indexed, not ignored. Asserted per extension, because an unrecognised file is not skipped visibly — it never enters the graph at all, and nothing reports its absence.
- **T35 — An unmatchable studio's videos relocate to the unfiled folder.** A non-personal asset whose studio is ruled out is placed in the shared unfiled folder — not left in root, and not given a folder of its own.
- **T36 — Deleting a video purges its pending tag associations.** No pending row survives the video it referred to, so a later classification cannot materialise an edge to a video that no longer exists.
- **T29 — A new file enters the same pipeline as a legacy one.** A file appearing after the migration arrives `unreviewed`, undeclared, unmatched and in the root, and proceeds through declaration, parsing, matching and relocation by the same code path — asserted by driving a new arrival and a legacy row through one flow and comparing the end states.
- **T30 — Deleting a video leaves every performer intact.** After deleting a video, each credited performer still exists with its profile, source id, photos and AKAs — **including a performer whose video count is now zero.** No cleanup pass removes it.
- **T31 — A missing file is never auto-deleted.** With the volume detached or a file removed externally, no asset record, edge or node is removed. The asset is reported missing and everything about it survives a re-scan.
- **T32 — Re-scanning changes nothing.** Running a scan twice over an unchanged library produces no new rows, no duplicate edges and no provenance churn.
- **T33 — A tombstoned entity is not resurrected.** An entity deleted by the operator stays deleted across a re-scan, a re-parse and a federation sync — asserted after v28's re-keying, not only before it.
- **T28 — A pending association resolves exactly once, and reports what it dropped.** Classifying a tag turns every pending association into an edge where the kind permits, discards the rest **with a report naming each video**, and leaves no pending row behind either way. Classifying into a name that already exists at that kind merges the nodes, re-points every pending row and edge, and leaves the unique index intact.
- **T27 — An unattended run creates no tag nodes.** A batch run writes no tag field and creates no node — `unclassified` or otherwise — nor any tag edge. Asserted directly against `VideoBatchPolicy.autoApplicableFields`, so the exclusion cannot be lost by a later refactor without failing.
- **T21 — Series survives as text.** `Asset.videoName` remains a free-text column through every migration phase; no node is created for it and no edge references it. Asserted because D1 deliberately declines to promote it, and a migration that promotes names to nodes is exactly the code that would sweep it up by accident.
- **T22 — Photos survive re-keying.** After the opaque-id migration, every profile and gallery image resolves for the node it belonged to, verified by count against the pre-migration set. A photo that no longer resolves is data loss, not a cache miss.
- **T23 — A failed move never costs a match.** Asserted separately for: volume detached, target-name collision, undeclared kind, **permission denied, disk full, and the source file missing at execution time**. In every case the match is persisted and readable, the file is untouched or restored, and the failure is reported. The last three are the ones a happy-path double never exercises and the ones a real 2,101-file run will actually hit.
- **T18b — A name becomes a legal path component, deterministically.** Names containing `/`, `:`, `\`, `?`, `*`, `"`, `<`, `>`, `|`, control characters and trailing dots or spaces all produce paths that are legal on macOS **and** Windows/SMB. The same name always yields the same component, two different names never collapse to the same one silently, and a name that sanitises to empty is skipped and reported rather than producing a path with an empty segment.
- **T24 — Relocation on match is reversible.** Every per-video move records old and new full paths, and replaying the mapping restores the original layout exactly — the same guarantee the bulk migration owes, at single-file granularity.
- **T18 — A generated path matches the ratified grammar, and personal content never reaches a studio folder.** For each content kind, the full path — folder and filename — matches the convention, resolves studio and performers through the validated lexicons, and places an unverified studio in the correct disposition. **Asserted explicitly: a ****`personal`**** video carrying a matched studio is filed in the personal folder, not under that studio.** This proves O1 here rather than deferring all of it to the child spec.

## What this Epic changes in the child specs
| Spec | Change |
| --- | --- |
| **File Naming & Metadata Storage Strategy** | Rewritten as derived. Its content classes and grammars stand; the model decisions it made locally move here. |
| **Filename Parsing & Bulk Rename Utility** | Rewritten as derived. D2 amended per D5 above. Its measured evidence — 2,101 files, 407 collisions, 1,048 with no identity metadata — carries forward unchanged. |
| **ViLM Plugin Architecture** | Amended: the provider contract must return and core must persist a candidate id for videos as well as performers; personal content excluded at the boundary. |

| **Plugin — Actor & Video Metadata Enrichment** | Amended: fetch-everything-on-match, and return the source id on the video path. |
